Let $H$ be a Hopf algebra over a field $k$ as in [[def-hh-hopf-algebra-and-antipode]], with multiplication, unit $1$, counit $\varepsilon$, and antipode. The **left-integral space** and **right-integral space** of $H$ are
$$
\int_H^\ell=\{\Lambda\in H:h\Lambda=\varepsilon(h)\Lambda\text{ for every }h\in H\},\qquad
\int_H^r=\{\Lambda\in H:\Lambda h=\varepsilon(h)\Lambda\text{ for every }h\in H\}.
$$
Both are linear subspaces and include zero. When $H$ is finite-dimensional, its dual $H^*$ is a Hopf algebra. Its product is convolution $(f*g)(h)=\sum f(h_1)g(h_2)$ and its counit is $\varepsilon_{H^*}(f)=f(1)$. A **left integral functional** on $H$ means an element $\lambda\in H^*$ satisfying $f*\lambda=f(1)\lambda$ for every $f\in H^*$; a **right integral functional** satisfies $\lambda*f=f(1)\lambda$. Zero is allowed in both definitions; existence of a nonzero integral is a theorem, not part of the definition.

Let $k$ be a field, $H$ a Hopf algebra over $k$, and $M$ a $k$-vector space. A **right $H$-module structure** on $M$ is a bilinear map $(m,h)\mapsto mh$ satisfying $(mh)g=m(hg)$ and $m1_H=m$. A **right $H$-comodule structure** is a linear map $\rho:M\to M\otimes H$ satisfying
$$
(\rho\otimes\operatorname{id}_H)\rho=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\Delta)\rho,\qquad (\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)\rho=\operatorname{id}_M.
$$
Write $\rho(m)=\sum m_0\otimes m_1$ and $\Delta(h)=\sum h_1\otimes h_2$, where each expression denotes a finite tensor sum. The pair of structures makes $M$ a **right-right Hopf module** if it satisfies
$$
\rho(mh)=\sum m_0h_1\otimes m_1h_2\qquad(m\in M,\ h\in H).
$$
A **morphism of right-right Hopf modules** is a linear map preserving both the right action and right coaction. The **coinvariants** are the subset
$$
M^{\operatorname{co}H}:=\{m\in M:\rho(m)=m\otimes1_H\}.
$$
The next lemma proves that this subset is a $k$-subspace. No finite-dimensionality of $H$ or $M$, and no bijectivity of the antipode, is part of the definition.

Let $V,W$ be finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces.

1. The bilinear map $V^*\times W^*\to(V\otimes W)^*$, $(f,g)\mapsto[v\otimes w\mapsto f(v)g(w)]$, induces an isomorphism $V^*\otimes W^*\to(V\otimes W)^*$. For ordered bases $(v_1,\dots,v_m)$ of $V$, $(w_1,\dots,w_n)$ of $W$ with dual bases $(v_i^*)$, $(w_j^*)$, the image of $v_i^*\otimes w_j^*$ is the dual basis vector of $v_i\otimes w_j$ in the product basis of $V\otimes W$.
2. For every ordered basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of $V$ the element $\sum_{i=1}^nv_i^*\otimes v_i\in V^*\otimes V$ is independent of the basis and corresponds to $\mathrm{id}_V$ under the isomorphism $V^*\otimes V\to\operatorname{Hom}(V,V)$, $f\otimes v\mapsto[x\mapsto f(x)v]$ ([[thm-hom-from-a-finite-dimensional-space-as-a-tensor-product]]). Its image under $\sigma_{V^*,V}$ is the corresponding element $\sum_iv_i\otimes v_i^*$ of $V\otimes V^*$.
3. The evaluation $\mathrm{ev}:V^*\otimes V\to k$, $f\otimes v\mapsto f(v)$, and the coevaluation $\mathrm{coev}:k\to V\otimes V^*$, $1\mapsto\sum_iv_i\otimes v_i^*$, are independent of the basis and satisfy $(\mathrm{id}_V\otimes\mathrm{ev})\circ\alpha_{V,V^*,V}\circ(\mathrm{coev}\otimes\mathrm{id}_V)=\mathrm{id}_V$ and $(\mathrm{ev}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{V^*})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{V^*,V,V^*}\circ(\mathrm{id}_{V^*}\otimes\mathrm{coev})=\mathrm{id}_{V^*}$, the unit isomorphisms $k\otimes V\cong V$, $V\otimes k\cong V$ being understood.

Let $H$ be a Hopf algebra over a field $k$, with antipode $S$, multiplication $m$, unit $u$, comultiplication $\Delta$, and counit $\varepsilon$. Then $S$ is unique, $S(1)=1$, and $\varepsilon\circ S=\varepsilon$. Moreover, for all $a,b\in H$,

$$S(ab)=S(b)S(a),\qquad \Delta(S(h))=(S\otimes S)\tau\Delta(h)\quad(h\in H),$$

where $\tau(x\otimes y)=y\otimes x$ is the tensor flip. In particular, these are consequences of the convolution-inverse definition; they are not extra axioms.

Let $k$ be a field and $H=(H,m,u,\Delta,\varepsilon,S)$ a finite-dimensional Hopf $k$-algebra. Give $H^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(H,k)$ the transposed Hopf structure: multiplication is convolution,
$$
(\phi\psi)(h)=(\phi\otimes\psi)(\Delta(h)),
$$
the unit is $\varepsilon$, coproduct is the transpose $m^*:H^*\to H^*\otimes H^*$ under finite tensor duality, the counit is $\phi\mapsto\phi(1_H)$, and the antipode is $S^*(\phi)=\phi\circ S$. Then $H^*$ is a Hopf algebra. No bijectivity assumption on $S$ is required.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional Hopf algebra over a field $k$. For $f\in H^*$ and $h,x\in H$, define
$$
(f\leftharpoonup h)(x)=f(xS(h)).
$$
For $f\in H^*$, define $\rho(f)=\sum f_0\otimes f_1\in H^*\otimes H$ by the requirement
$$
\sum p(f_1)f_0(x)=\sum p(x_1)f(x_2)\qquad(p\in H^*,\ x\in H).
$$

Let $H$ be a Hopf algebra over a field $k$ and $M$ a right-right Hopf module over $H$. Equip $M^{\operatorname{co}H}\otimes H$ with the free right-right Hopf-module structure. The map
$$
\alpha:M^{\operatorname{co}H}\otimes H\to M,\qquad n\otimes h\mapsto nh,
$$
is an isomorphism of right-right Hopf modules, with inverse
$$
\beta:M\to M^{\operatorname{co}H}\otimes H,\qquad \beta(m)=\sum P(m_0)\otimes m_1,
$$
where $P(m)=\sum m_0S(m_1)$. No bijectivity assumption on $S$ is used.

For a finite-dimensional unital associative $k$-algebra $A$, the full dual $A^*$ is a coalgebra under the transpose of multiplication and unit. For every coalgebra $C$, the full dual $C^*$ is a unital associative algebra under convolution. These dualizations reverse algebra and coalgebra maps. Restricted to finite-dimensional objects, the two contravariant dualizations are inverse equivalences via the canonical evaluation maps $A\to A^{**}$ and $C\to C^{**}$. The finite-dimensionality hypothesis in the algebra-to-coalgebra direction is on $A$ itself, not merely on a module over $A$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$
If $B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)$ is a basis of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space $V$, then its dual family $B^*=(b_1^*,\ldots,b_n^*)$ is a basis of $V^*$. Consequently $\dim V^*=\dim V=n$.

citations.quote: Let $k$ be a field, $N>1$, and $\zeta\in k$ a primitive $N$-th root of unity, with $\operatorname{char}(k)\nmid N$. On the $N^2$-dimensional vector space with basis $g^i x^j$, $0\le i,j<N$, define multiplication on basis elements by $(g^i x^j)(g^a x^b)=\zeta^{-aj}g^{\,i+a\ {\rm mod}\ N}x^{j+b}$ if $j+b<N$, and by $0$ if $j+b\ge N$. Then this is an associative unital algebra and is the presented algebra $k\langle g,x\rangle/(g^N-1,\ x^N,\ gx-\zeta xg)$; the displayed basis is a basis of that quotient. It becomes a Hopf algebra with $\Delta(g)=g\otimes g$, $\Delta(x)=1\otimes x+x\otimes g$, $\varepsilon(g)=1$, $\varepsilon(x)=0$, $S(g)=g^{-1}$, and $S(x)=-xg^{-1}$.

Let $k$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital associative $k$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A bilinear form $\beta:A\times A\to k$ is **associative** when $\beta(ab,c)=\beta(a,bc)$ for all $a,b,c\in A$. It is **nondegenerate** when both linear maps
$$
A\to A^*,\qquad a\mapsto[b\mapsto\beta(a,b)],\qquad b\mapsto[a\mapsto\beta(a,b)]
$$
are isomorphisms. A linear functional $\lambda:A\to k$ is a **Frobenius functional** when $\beta_\lambda(a,b):=\lambda(ab)$ is nondegenerate. Associativity of $\beta_\lambda$ follows from associativity of multiplication. The algebra $A$ is **Frobenius** when it has at least one Frobenius functional.

Set $H^{\otimes3}:=(H\otimes H)\otimes H$. Define linear maps
$\iota_{12}(a\otimes b)=(a\otimes b)\otimes1_H,\qquad \iota_{13}(a\otimes b)=(a\otimes1_H)\otimes b,\qquad \iota_{23}(a\otimes b)=(1_H\otimes a)\otimes b.$
For $X\in H\otimes H$, write $X_{ij}:=\iota_{ij}(X)$ and $X_{21}:=\tau_{H,H}(X)$, where $\tau_{H,H}(a\otimes b)=b\otimes a$. Define $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}:=\tau_{H,H}\circ\Delta$. In the second hexagon below, $\alpha^{-1}_{H,H,H}$ is the canonical reassociation $(H\otimes(H\otimes H))\to((H\otimes H)\otimes H)$ from [F4].

An algebraic quasitriangular structure on $H$ is an invertible element $R\in H\otimes H$ such that, for every $h\in H$,
$R\Delta(h)=\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}(h)R,$
and
$(\Delta\otimes\operatorname{id}_H)(R)=R_{13}R_{23},\qquad \alpha^{-1}_{H,H,H}(\operatorname{id}_H\otimes\Delta)(R)=R_{13}R_{12}.$
All products are in the componentwise tensor-product algebra, and $R$ is a finite algebraic tensor sum. The displayed formula with $\alpha^{-1}$ is the parenthesized form of $(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)R=R_{13}R_{12}$.

Let $H$ be a Hopf algebra over a field $k$ and let $H\text{-Mod}$ denote the category of all left $H$-modules and all $H$-linear maps, with tensor action and associators as in [[def-hh-module-category-and-tensor-action]] and [[thm-hh-bialgebra-module-tensor-coherence]]. A braiding on this category is a family of $H$-linear isomorphisms
$c_{V,W}:V\otimes W\longrightarrow W\otimes V$
for all left $H$-modules $V,W$, natural in both variables, for which the following equalities hold after inserting the canonical associators of the module category:
$c_{U,V\otimes W}=(\operatorname{id}_V\otimes c_{U,W})\circ(c_{U,V}\otimes\operatorname{id}_W),\qquad c_{U\otimes V,W}=(c_{U,W}\otimes\operatorname{id}_V)\circ(\operatorname{id}_U\otimes c_{V,W}).$
A quasitriangular structure $R$ is triangular if $R_{21}R=1_H\otimes1_H$. A braiding is symmetric if $c_{W,V}\circ c_{V,W}=\operatorname{id}_{V\otimes W}$ for every $V,W$. No finite-dimensional restriction is imposed on $H$ or on the modules in $H\text{-Mod}$.

Let $k$ be a field and let $H$ be a $k$-vector space with associative unital multiplication $m$, unit $1_H$, coassociative comultiplication $Delta:H\to H\otimes_k H$, and counit $\varepsilon:H\to k$. Assume $\Delta$ and $\varepsilon$ are unital algebra maps; this is the bialgebra interface used on this page. A left $H$-module is a unital left module in the sense of [[def-left-and-right-modules]]: its action satisfies $1_Hv=v$ and $(hh')v=h(h'v)$. Let $H\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$ be the category whose objects are all left $H$-modules and whose morphisms $f:V\to W$ are $k$-linear maps satisfying $f(hv)=h f(v)$ for every $h\in H$ and $v\in V$.

For left $H$-modules $V,W$, give the algebraic tensor product $V\otimes_k W$ the candidate action

$$h\cdot(v\otimes w)=\sum h_{(1)}v\otimes h_{(2)}w,\qquad \Delta(h)=\sum h_{(1)}\otimes h_{(2)}.$$

The sums are finite algebraic tensor sums; the tensor product and scalar conventions are those of [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. The candidate unit object is $k_\varepsilon=k$ with $h\cdot c=\varepsilon(h)c$. For morphisms $f:V\to V'$ and $g:W\to W'$, the candidate tensor morphism is the usual linear map $f\otimes g$ determined by $(f\otimes g)(v\otimes w)=f(v)\otimes g(w)$ through [[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]].

These formulas specify the proposed tensor operations; [[thm-hh-bialgebra-module-tensor-coherence]] proves that they are module actions and that the canonical associator and unit maps are morphisms in $H\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$.

Let $k$ be a field, $H$ a unital associative $k$-algebra, and $\Delta:H\to H\otimes_k H$ and $\varepsilon:H\to k$ linear maps. Suppose first that $H$ is a bialgebra: $\Delta$ is coassociative and a unital algebra map, and $\varepsilon$ is a counit and a unital algebra map. For the category $H\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$ and candidate tensor action of [[def-hh-module-category-and-tensor-action]], the tensor product of two left $H$-modules is a left $H$-module, $k_\varepsilon$ is the unit module, tensor products of $H$-linear maps are $H$-linear, and the canonical associator and unit maps are $H$-linear. They are natural, and the pentagon and triangle diagrams commute. Thus these operations define a monoidal category of left $H$-modules; no symmetry or braiding is asserted.

Conversely, start with only the unital associative algebra $H$ and the linear maps $\Delta,\varepsilon$. If the displayed formula of [[def-hh-module-category-and-tensor-action]] makes $V\otimes_k W$ a left $H$-module for every pair of left $H$-modules, $k_\varepsilon$ is a left $H$-module, and the canonical associator and both canonical unit maps are $H$-linear, then $\Delta$ is a coassociative counital unital algebra map and $\varepsilon$ is a counital unital algebra map. Hence these data make $H$ a bialgebra.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A$ be a unital $R$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]), with $A$ regarded as its left regular module.

1. For $a,b\in A$ one has $a=b$ if and only if $a\cdot1_A=b\cdot1_A$.
2. For $n\ge1$ the tensor power $A^{\otimes n}$ is a left $A$-module via $a\cdot(a_1\otimes\cdots\otimes a_n)=(aa_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes a_n$. If $a\cdot z=b\cdot z$ for all $z\in A^{\otimes n}$, then $a=b$; in particular the single element $1_A^{\otimes n}$ detects equality. The analogous statement holds for the right regular structure. The empty tensor power $A^{\otimes0}=R$ carries no canonical left $A$-module structure here, so no $n=0$ case is claimed.
3. For $n\ge1$, if $f,g:A^{\times n}\to M$ are $R$-multilinear and agree on every $n$-tuple, then the $R$-linear maps $A^{\otimes n}\to M$ they induce ([[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]) agree; conversely, agreement of the induced maps gives agreement on all pure tensors $a_1\otimes\cdots\otimes a_n$.
4. Descent warning: if $\pi:A\to A/I$ is a quotient of $R$-algebras ([[thm-quotient-ring-universal-property]]), the induced map $A^{\otimes n}\to(A/I)^{\otimes n}$ is surjective, but an identity between $R$-linear maps out of $(A/I)^{\otimes n}$ may be checked on images of pure tensors of $A$ only after those maps have been shown to be well defined on the quotient; surjectivity alone is not descent.

Let $H$ be a Hopf algebra over a field $k$ and let $R\in H\otimes H$ be invertible and satisfy the quasitriangular axioms of [[def-hh-leg-notation-and-quasitriangular-hopf-algebra]]. Then
$(\varepsilon\otimes\operatorname{id})(R)=1_H=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\varepsilon)(R),$
and
$R_{12}R_{13}R_{23}=R_{23}R_{13}R_{12}\quad\text{in }H^{\otimes3}.$

Let $A$ be a unital algebra over a field $k$. For $n=2,3$, give $A^{\otimes n}$ its iterated componentwise tensor-product algebra structure and unit $1_A^{\otimes n}$. If $X,Y\in A^{\otimes n}$ and left multiplication by $X$ and $Y$ agree as maps $A^{\otimes n}\to A^{\otimes n}$, then $X=Y$. In particular, evaluation of a left-multiplication operator at $1_A^{\otimes n}$ recovers the tensor that defines it.

derivations.claim: Write $R=\sum_i a_i\otimes b_i$. The left action of $H\otimes H$ on $V\otimes W$ sends $(a\otimes b)(v\otimes w)$ to $av\otimes bw$; therefore the finite tensor $R$ defines the linear map in the Statement, independently of its chosen sum representation. Its inverse is $(\rho_V\otimes\rho_W)(R^{-1})\circ\tau_{W,V}$, so $c_{V,W}$ is an isomorphism.

Now suppose a braiding is given on all left $H$-modules. For $v\in V$, the map $f_v:H\to V$, $x\mapsto xv$, is $H$-linear because module associativity gives $f_v(hx)=(hx)v=h(xv)$, and [F5] gives $f_v(1_H)=v$. Set $R=\tau_{H,H}c_{H,H}(1_H\otimes1_H)$. Naturality for $f_v$ and $f_w$ then gives $c_{V,W}(v\otimes w)=\sum_i b_iw\otimes a_iv$ when $R=\sum_i a_i\otimes b_i$.

For $h\in H$, the diagonal tensor action and the quasitriangular relation give $c_{V,W}\rho_{V\otimes W}(h)=\tau_{V,W}(\rho_V\otimes\rho_W)(R\Delta(h)) =\tau_{V,W}(\rho_V\otimes\rho_W)(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}(h)R) =\rho_{W\otimes V}(h)c_{V,W},$ where the last equality is the elementary flip identity $\tau\rho_{V,W}(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}(h))=\rho_{W,V}(h)\tau$. Hence $c_{V,W}$ is $H$-linear.

If $f:V\to V'$ and $g:W\to W'$ are $H$-linear, then $(g\otimes f)c_{V,W}$ and $c_{V',W'}(f\otimes g)$ both send $v\otimes w$ to $\sum_i b_i g(w)\otimes a_i f(v)$, using the $H$-linearity of $f,g$. Thus the family is natural.

On $u\otimes v\otimes w$, the map $c_{U,V\otimes W}$ gives $\sum_i (b_i)_{(1)}v\otimes(b_i)_{(2)}w\otimes a_i u$. The second hexagon identity rewrites this coefficient tensor as $R_{13}R_{12}=\sum_{j,k}a_ja_k\otimes b_k\otimes b_j$, so the result is $\sum_{j,k}b_kv\otimes b_jw\otimes a_ja_ku$, exactly $(\operatorname{id}_V\otimes c_{U,W})(c_{U,V}\otimes\operatorname{id}_W)(u\otimes v\otimes w)$. Equality on spanning pure tensors proves the first hexagon.

On $u\otimes v\otimes w$, the map $c_{U\otimes V,W}$ gives $\sum_i b_iw\otimes(a_i)_{(1)}u\otimes(a_i)_{(2)}v$. Its boxes are triples $(c,a,b)$ with $1\le c\le r$, $a\ge1$, and $1\le b\le\lambda^{(c)}_a$. Order the boxes within component $c$ by the transitive closure of $(c,a,b)<(c,a,b+1)$ and $(c,a,b)<(c,a+1,b)$; boxes in different components are incomparable.

A **standard multitableau** $t$ of shape $\lambda$ is a bijective filling of the boxes by $1,\ldots,n$ that increases along every row and column. Equivalently, it is a linear extension of this finite box poset. Write $\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$ for the set of such fillings and

$$ \operatorname{res}_t(i)=u_cQ^{b-a}\quad\text{if entry }i\text{ occupies }(c,a,b). $$

The **generic content field** is $K=\mathbb Q(Q,u_1,\ldots,u_r)$, the fraction field of $R$. The contents of distinct addable boxes of any multipartition are distinct in $K$. If two boxes in one component have the same content, they lie on one diagonal; the right and lower boxes immediately between them are distinct required predecessors of the southeast box. Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let $e=e(F,q)$ and assume $e>n$ (with $e=\infty$ allowed); let $\lambda\vdash n$, $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$, and let $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ be the Murphy cell module with Murphy basis $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

1. (**Separation**) If $s,t$ are standard $\lambda$-tableaux with $[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$ for all $1\le k\le n$ then $s=t$. More precisely, if the q-content values agree for all $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$ for some $i$, then $s=t$ or $t=s(i\ i+1)$. 2. (**Idempotents**) Let $\mathcal R_k$ be the set of distinct q-content values of the entry $k$ over standard tableaux of **all** partitions of $n$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ define $$F_t:=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\ \prod_{\substack{c\in\mathcal R_k\\        c\ne[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q}}        \frac{L_k-c}{[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q-c}\in F[L_1,\ldots,L_n].$$ These are orthogonal idempotents of $H$; their actions on $S_{\mathrm M}^\lambda$ project onto the corresponding simultaneous eigenlines. Put $f_t=m_tF_t$. Then $f_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_qf_t$ and $f_t=m_t+\sum_{s\rhd t}a_sm_s$. The global content sets are essential for the asserted idempotency in $H$, rather than only the induced same-shape endomorphisms. 3. (**Orthogonal seminormal basis**) $\{f_t:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is a basis of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ satisfying $f_tF_s=\delta_{ts}f_t$ and $\langle f_s,f_t\rangle_\lambda=\delta_{st}\langle f_t,f_t\rangle_\lambda$; it is the **seminormal basis** of the Murphy cell module. 4. (**Generator action**) Let $s$ be a standard $\lambda$-tableau, $1\le i<n$ and $t:=s(i\ i+1)$, and put $\rho:=\operatorname{content}_s(i)-\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)\in\mathbb Z$. If $i$ and $i+1$ lie in the same row of $s$ then $f_sT_i=q\,f_s$; if they lie in the same column then $f_sT_i=-f_s$; otherwise $t$ is standard and $$f_sT_i=\alpha_i(s)\,f_t-\frac{1}{[\rho]_q}f_s,\qquad \alpha_i(s):=\begin{cases}1,&s\rhd t,\\[1mm]\dfrac{[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q}{[\rho]_q[-\rho]_q},&t\rhd s,\end{cases}$$ where $[-\rho]_q$ is the extended quantum integer of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]] and for the swapped tableau $\operatorname{content}_t(i)-\operatorname{content}_t(i+1)=-\rho$. No semisimplicity of $H$ is assumed and no choice principle is used.

Fix $r,n\ge1$ and work in the universal cyclotomic algebra $H_{r,n}$ of [[def-hh-multiplicative-cyclotomic-hecke-algebra]], with parameters $Q,u_1,\ldots,u_r$, commuting Jucys–Murphy generators $L_i=X_i$, and finite generators $T_i$. For an $r$-multipartition $\lambda$, put $a_c=\sum_{d<c}|\lambda^{(d)}|$ and define
$$u_\lambda=\prod_{c=2}^{r}\ \prod_{i=1}^{a_c}(L_i-u_c).$$
Let $t^\lambda$ be the row-standard initial multitableau from [[def-hh-cell-datum-dominance-and-cell-ideals]]. Let $S_\lambda$ be the subgroup of $S_n$ that permutes labels within each row of $t^\lambda$, and set $x_\lambda=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w$ and $m_\lambda=u_\lambda x_\lambda$. The anti-involution $*$ is the generator-fixing map of [[lem-hh-cyclotomic-anti-involution-fixes-generators]].

For a standard multitableau $t$, use the right entry action $t\cdot w:=w^{-1}\cdot t$, where the left action applies $w$ to every entry. Let $d(t)$ be the unique permutation with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Standardness implies that $d(t)$ is the distinguished minimal representative for its row-stabilizer coset. For standard $s,t$ of shape $\lambda$, define
$$m_{st}=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}.$$
These are specified elements of $H_{r,n}$; this definition does not assert their linear independence or cellularity.

Fix $r,n\ge1$ and use the independent units $Q,u_1,\ldots,u_r$ of [[def-hh-multiplicative-cyclotomic-hecke-algebra]]. An **$r$-multipartition** of $n$ is a tuple $\lambda=(\lambda^{(1)},\ldots,\lambda^{(r)})$ of ordinary partitions whose total number of boxes is $n$. Its boxes are triples $(c,a,b)$ with $1\le c\le r$, $a\ge1$, and $1\le b\le\lambda^{(c)}_a$. Order the boxes within component $c$ by the transitive closure of $(c,a,b)<(c,a,b+1)$ and $(c,a,b)<(c,a+1,b)$; boxes in different components are incomparable.

A **standard multitableau** $t$ of shape $\lambda$ is a bijective filling of the boxes by $1,\ldots,n$ that increases along every row and column. Equivalently, it is a linear extension of this finite box poset. Write $\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$ for the set of such fillings and

$$ \operatorname{res}_t(i)=u_cQ^{b-a}\quad\text{if entry }i\text{ occupies }(c,a,b). $$

The **generic content field** is $K=\mathbb Q(Q,u_1,\ldots,u_r)$, the fraction field of $R$. The contents of distinct addable boxes of any multipartition are distinct in $K$. If two boxes in one component have the same content, they lie on one diagonal; the right and lower boxes immediately between them are distinct required predecessors of the southeast box. Consequently, for three consecutive labels $i,i+1,i+2$ in a standard multitableau, the first and third contents cannot agree. In particular every pair of contents among three consecutive labels is distinct in $K$. If two boxes in one component have content exponents differing by $1$, then they are comparable in the box order, so interchanging adjacent labels in a standard multitableau never gives a content ratio $Q$ or $Q^{-1}$.

Let $R_A=\mathbb Z[Q^{\pm1}]$ and let $H_n$ be the type-A Hecke algebra on $T_1,\ldots,T_{n-1}$ with braid relations and $(T_i-Q)(T_i+1)=0$. For a partition $\lambda\vdash n$, let $t^\lambda$ be row-filled, $S_\lambda$ its row subgroup, $x_\lambda=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w$, and
$$m_{st}=T_{d(s)}^*x_\lambda T_{d(t)}$$
for standard $\lambda$-tableaux, with the tableau action and distinguished representatives fixed in [[def-hh-cyclotomic-murphy-elements]]. Then the $m_{st}$ form an $R_A$-basis of $H_n$, $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$, and the spans $H_n^{\trianglerighteq\lambda}$ and $H_n^{\triangleright\lambda}$ of shapes respectively dominating and strictly dominating $\lambda$ are two-sided ideals. For every $h\in H_n$ and standard $s,t$ of shape $\lambda$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_{t,v}(h)m_{sv}\pmod{H_n^{\triangleright\lambda}},$$
where $r_{t,v}(h)\in R_A$ does not depend on $s$. The proof is integral over $R_A$; it does not divide by $Q+1$ or assume semisimplicity.

derivations.claim: Work first over $K$. For standard $u,v$ of shape $\mu$, define the endomorphism $R_{uv}$ by $wR_{uv}=\langle w,f_u\rangle f_v$ on $W_\mu$, and by zero on other $W_\nu$. Nonsingularity makes these a basis of $\bigoplus_\mu\operatorname{End}_K(W_\mu)$. The faithful action map of [F2] is a $K$-linear isomorphism onto this endomorphism space because its dimensions agree. Thus the $R_{uv}$ are coordinates for $H_{n,K}$. Invariance gives $w(T_iR_{uv})=\langle w,f_uT_i\rangle f_v$ and $w(R_{uv}T_i)=\langle w,f_u\rangle(f_vT_i)$. Left multiplication therefore changes only $u$, right multiplication only $v$, and each changes its index only to itself or its standard adjacent swap; both directions of a standard swap have nonzero coefficients.

We need a comparison valid across shapes. Let $b$ be row standard with $i$ in an upper row and $i+1$ in a lower row, and put $b'=b(i,i+1)$. If standard $a\unrhd_{\rm tab}b$, then $a\unrhd_{\rm tab}b'$ and every standard swap $a'=a(i,i+1)$ also dominates $b'$. Only the cutoff $m=i$ changes. A swap raising $a$'s counts causes no problem. For a lowering swap, a failure at row cutoff $j$ would require $A_a(j,i)=A_b(j,i)$ while $b$'s swap does not lower its count at $j$. If both labels lie above $j$ in $b$, then $A_a(j,i+1)=A_b(j,i)<A_b(j,i+1)$, contradicting $a\unrhd_{\rm tab}b$. If both lie below $j$, then $A_a(j,i-1)=A_b(j,i)-1<A_b(j,i-1)$, again a contradiction. These exhaust the possible failures.

Let $B_r$ be the interval of labels occupying row $r$ of $t^\alpha$, and write $x_\alpha=\sum a_{uv}R_{uv}$. Fix a right index $v$ and an adjacent pair $i,i+1$ inside $B_r$. Comparing coefficients in $T_ix_\alpha=Qx_\alpha$, if $i,i+1$ share a column of $u$, gives $-a_{uv}=Qa_{uv}$; no other first index can contribute because $u(i,i+1)$ is not standard. Hence $a_{uv}=0$. If $u'=u(i,i+1)$ is standard, its coefficient equation has the form $Qa_{uv}=c_ua_{uv}+a_{u'}a_{u'v}$, where $a_{u'}\ne0$ is the seminormal off-diagonal scalar. Thus $a_{uv}=0$ forces $a_{u'v}=0$, and the reverse implication follows from the equation at $u'$. Zeros therefore propagate across every standard swap inside a block $B_r$.

Replace each label of $u$ in $B_r$ by $r$, obtaining a weakly increasing row and column tableau $S$. The standard refinements of a fixed $S$ are the linear extensions of the node-order posets in its equal-label classes. Any two linear extensions of a finite poset are connected by adjacent incomparable swaps: move the first desired element left across its predecessors in the other extension, all of which must be incomparable, and continue inductively. Here these are standard swaps of consecutive integers inside a block $B_r$. If $S$ repeats a label in a column, weak column order supplies vertically adjacent equal-label nodes, a cover pair $x<y$ in that class. A cover pair occurs consecutively in some linear extension: first extend the order ideal $\{z:z<y,\ z\ne x\}$, then place $x,y$, then complete; the displayed set is an ideal because $x<z<y$ would contradict the cover condition. This refinement has consecutive labels in one column, so step 2.1 and connectivity force every coefficient in its fibre to vanish. Therefore every supported $u$ refines a column-strict, hence semistandard, $S$.

A positive-integer column-strict tableau has label at least its row index. Put $b_j=\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_j$. Every entry $1,\ldots,b_j$ in a surviving refinement $u$ therefore lies in its first $j$ rows, giving $A_u(j,m)\ge\min(m,b_j)=A_{t^\alpha}(j,m)$ for all $j,m$. The right parabolic equation and the same argument give $v\unrhd_{\rm tab}t^\alpha$. Also choose the $k$ row labels whose multiplicities are the $k$ largest parts of $\alpha$. Column-strictness permits at most $k$ chosen labels per column, so their total multiplicity is at most $\sum_c\min(k,\operatorname{height}(c))=\mu_1+\cdots+\mu_k$. Thus each surviving spectral shape satisfies $\mu\unrhd\bar\alpha$.

Choose a reduced expression $d(s)=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$. Every reduced prefix is a distinguished row representative: write $d(s)=ab$ with $a$ that prefix and $\ell(d(s))=\ell(a)+\ell(b)$. If $a$ were not minimal in its left row coset, some $y\in S_\alpha$ would have $\ell(ya)<\ell(a)$, giving $\ell(yd(s))\le\ell(ya)+\ell(b)<\ell(d(s))$, contrary to the minimality of $d(s)$. Hence $b_r=t^\alpha s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_r}$ is row standard, and each step moves $i_r$ from an upper row to a lower one. Apply $T_{i_1},\ldots,T_{i_k}$ successively on the left of $x_\alpha$. Their final product is $T_{d(s)}^*x_\alpha$. By steps 1.1 and 1.2, spectral indices initially dominating $t^\alpha$ continue to dominate $b_r$ at each stage; an unchanged index also works because $b_{r-1}\unrhd_{\rm tab}b_r$. The right index and shape do not change. Applying the right-handed argument along a reduced word of $d(t)$ now proves that the spectral expansion of $m^\alpha_{st}$ has support only at $R_{uv}$ with $u\unrhd_{\rm tab}s$, $v\unrhd_{\rm tab}t$, and shape dominating $\bar\alpha$.

Let $P$ be the finite set of pairs of standard tableaux of a common shape, ordered by $(u,v)\ge(s,t)$ when both tableau-prefix comparisons hold. This is a partial order across shapes: equality of all counts determines the row of each label, hence the row-standard tableau. Apply step 5.1 to every standard Murphy element. Its transition matrix $C$ to the spectral basis has entry zero unless its output pair dominates its input pair. Both families are bases by [F1] and step 1.1, so $C$ is invertible. In a linear extension of $P$ it is triangular, hence its diagonal part $D$ is invertible. Write $C=D(I+N)$; $N$ has only strict-order entries, so $N^{|P|}=0$, since a nonzero product would require a strict chain with $|P|+1$ elements. Therefore $C^{-1}=(I-N+\cdots+(-N)^{|P|-1})D^{-1}$. Every term has the same ordered-pair support, because the partial order is transitive. Each $R_{uv}$ thus expands only in $m_{wz}$ with $w\unrhd_{\rm tab}u$, $z\unrhd_{\rm tab}v$.

Substitute these inverse transitions into step 5.1. Every surviving standard Murphy term has $w\unrhd_{\rm tab}u\unrhd_{\rm tab}s$ and $z\unrhd_{\rm tab}v\unrhd_{\rm tab}t$. At the final label cutoff $n$, $w\unrhd_{\rm tab}u$ implies that its shape dominates the shape of $u$, so the shape also dominates $\bar\alpha$. This proves all assertions over $K$. By [F1] the unique standard-Murphy coordinates of $m^\alpha_{st}$ already lie in $A$; injectivity of $A\hookrightarrow K$ makes every coordinate proved zero over $K$ equal to zero in $A$. The resulting integral identities specialize under any map $A\to R$ sending $Q$ to a unit. No semisimplicity or quantum-integer division is required in $R$.
